title: From logits to a decision - argmax, sampling and generation

questions.prompt: What is the decisive difference between a chat LLM and a decision model at the decoding step?
options: The chat LLM uses softmax and the decision model uses argmax

The chat LLM decodes over an open vocabulary of tokens and generates a sequence by feeding each sampled token back; the decision model decodes over your fixed list of options and produces one distribution, once
The decision model runs more blocks than the chat LLM
The chat LLM returns probabilities and the decision model returns text
questions.explain: Both use the same softmax. The chat LLM's vocabulary is tens of thousands of tokens and the loop runs until a stop condition; the decision model's vocabulary is the criteria you listed in the question and there is no loop - one softmax, one distribution. The tempting wrong answer is the fourth one, which is exactly backwards: the decision model returns probabilities and a value, and the chat LLM returns text.

questions.prompt: What does raising the temperature from 1.0 to 5.0 do to a distribution over options?
options: It flattens the distribution - the top option's probability falls - but it never changes the RANKING of the options
It sharpens the distribution, because dividing by a bigger number makes the logits larger
It changes the ranking, because the smaller gaps get relatively bigger
It leaves the distribution untouched, because softmax normalises away any constant
questions.explain: Temperature divides the logits before the softmax, so a bigger T makes the gaps between logits smaller in the exponent and the distribution flatter. The ranking is untouched - examples/02_temperature.py asserts that the order is preserved at every temperature. The tempting wrong answer is the third one: raising T never reorders anything, it only changes how lopsided the distribution is.

questions.prompt: The model returns {"billing": 0.72, "technical": 0.18, "sales": 0.10}. If you sample from this distribution many times, roughly what fraction of draws give "billing"?
options: About 10%, because sampling is uniform over the options
About 50%, because the top two options are close
About 72%, because each option is drawn in proportion to its probability
About 100%, because billing is the argmax
questions.explain: Sampling draws in proportion to the probabilities, so billing comes up roughly 72% of the time. The tempting wrong answer is the fourth one: that is argmax, not sampling, and it is a different decoding strategy that throws away the rest of the distribution.

questions.prompt: Why does this repo measure the probabilities dict rather than the chosen option?
options: Because the probabilities are cheaper for the provider to compute
Because the probabilities carry the information a hard label throws away, and they are what the threshold and the calibration metrics need
Because the chosen option is often wrong
Because the harness cannot store strings in JSON
questions.explain: decisionarena/metrics.py's collect_scored() pulls the probability of the gold option out of the dict, and action_change_rate() compares the top probability against the threshold. Both need the distribution, not the label. The tempting wrong answer is the third one: the label is right most of the time - but the whole point is that a hard label cannot tell you whether the model was barely right or overwhelmingly right, and that distinction is what calibration is made of.

questions.prompt: In cases/routing.json, the thresholds are {"is_billing": 0.5, "team": 0.6, "severity": 0.5}. What does that 0.6 mean for the team question?
options: The routing decision is made only if the model's top team probability is at least 0.6
The model must assign exactly 0.6 to the billing team
60% of the team question's tokens are used as context
The model's confidence must be 0.6, independently of the option probabilities
questions.explain: The threshold is the decision rule that sits between the distribution and the action: metrics.action_change_rate() acts when the top probability clears it. The tempting wrong answer is the last one - confidence is a separate field from the probabilities, and the harness acts on the probabilities, not on the reported confidence.
